strengths: The paper identifies two concrete and plausible failure modes of TTFS-coded SNNs (signal diminishing with depth and imbalanced membrane potential distribution) and supports these observations with visualizations (firing rate, membrane potential histograms, gradient magnitude plots).

The proposed variance-based initialization is derived analytically from the specific input statistics of TTFS neurons (single-spike constraint over T steps), which is a reasonable and interpretable extension of Kaiming-style analysis to spiking/binary signals.
The ablation study (Table III) isolates the contribution of initialization vs. average pooling, showing incremental accuracy gains from each component.
The paper offers a clear intuitive argument for why average pooling is more compatible with the TTFS single-spike-sum invariant than max pooling, backed by a short derivation (Eqs. 24-25).
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST with very shallow architectures (2-3 layer MLPs/small CNNs); no results on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, or neuromorphic datasets (DVS-Gesture, CIFAR10-DVS) commonly used in this literature, which severely limits evidence that the method scales or generalizes to harder tasks or deeper networks (despite claims that the method solves depth-related problems).

The MNIST result of 99.2% is marked with an asterisk in Table I with no accompanying footnote or explanation anywhere in the text, and this number is presented as beating TQTTFS's 98.6% while the abstract/body text elsewhere states ETTFS reaches 98.2% — internal inconsistency between text (98.2%) and table (99.2%) that is never resolved, undermining confidence in the reported SOTA claims.

No experiments demonstrating the claimed 'accelerates the training process' / 'fewer time steps' advantage in a quantified, comparable way against baselines (e.g., actual wall-clock or iteration-count comparisons against competing TTFS methods at matched accuracy); Figs 8-9 only show before/after-init curves on the authors' own model, not comparisons to prior work.

The derivation of the initialization (Section III-C) assumes exactly one spike per neuron over the time window and treats spikes as i.i.d. across inputs j to compute variance (n independent Bernoulli-like terms), which is inconsistent with the TTFS single-spike-per-neuron constraint that induces strong dependence among S^{l-1}[t][j] across j (only one of them can be firing at a given t across the population is not enforced, but across time for a given neuron exactly one fires) — the paper does not adequately justify treating these as independent for computing D(X^l), leaving the theoretical derivation on shaky footing.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed runs are reported for any of the results in Tables I-III or Figures 8-9, making it impossible to assess whether the improvements (e.g., 90.1% vs 89.3%, or 91.61% vs 90.35%) are statistically meaningful versus run-to-run variance.

The related-work/comparison baselines (S4NN, BS4NN, STDBP, TQTTFS) are several years old (2019-2024) but the paper does not compare against more recent competitive direct-training SNN methods with normalization/BN-based initializations (e.g., threshold-dependent BN, RecDis-SNN mentioned in related work) despite discussing them, so it is unclear if simpler existing fixes (e.g., BN, RecDis-SNN's distribution rectification) would already resolve the same issues without the proposed changes.

The temporal weighting decoding method (Sec III-D) is presented with a fixed scaling factor gamma=2 chosen seemingly ad hoc, and while an ablation on gamma is promised ('Sec IV-C'), Table III (the actual ablation) does not include any ablation on the temporal weighting scheme itself, decay function choice, or gamma sensitivity, despite this being highlighted as a core contribution.

Presentation issues: duplicate/mislabeled figure captions (Fig. 9 caption is identical to Fig. 8's caption, 'Comparison of the convergence speed and final performance of the network', despite showing firing rate not accuracy), and repeated conference formatting artifacts (e.g., 'TABLE III' 'diminishing' misspelled as 'disminishing' multiple times), reducing overall polish and clarity.

The claimed generality of the framework is undercut by the fact all experiments use only IF/simple neuron models on simple grayscale digit datasets; no discussion or test of whether the initialization/pooling insights hold for LIF neurons, deeper conv-nets, or more realistic vision benchmarks limits the significance of the contribution to the broader SNN community.

strengths: The paper provides a reasonably clear theoretical derivation connecting variance-preserving initialization principles to the specific signal statistics of TTFS-coded spikes, extending the Kaiming-style analysis to account for the single-spike-per-neuron and temporal averaging assumptions.

The empirical diagnostics (firing rate decay, membrane potential distribution skew, near-zero weight gradients under Kaiming init) are plausible, visually presented, and consistent with the stated problems of signal diminishing and imbalanced potential distribution.
The argument for replacing max-pooling with average-pooling is intuitive and grounded in the single-spike/TTFS output constraint, and the accompanying derivation (Eqs. 24-25) is easy to follow.
The ablation in Table III shows each proposed component (init, avg-pooling) contributes incrementally to the reported final accuracy.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted entirely to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, both near-saturated toy benchmarks; no results on CIFAR-10/100, neuromorphic datasets (e.g., DVS-Gesture, CIFAR10-DVS), or any deeper/more realistic architecture are shown, despite the motivating analysis explicitly discussing deeper networks (Fig. 4, 5-layer net) and general TTFS scalability claims. This severely limits the demonstrated significance and generality of the contribution.

There is a clear numerical inconsistency between the text and Table I: the text states "ETTFS method achieves an accuracy of 98.2%", while Table I reports "99.2*%" with an unexplained asterisk, and the two values disagree with each other as well as with the surrounding SOTA comparison narrative. This undermines confidence in the reported results and suggests inadequate proofreading/verification.

The abstract and title emphasize an "efficient training framework" that "accelerates training," yet no wall-clock time, FLOPs, memory, or spike-count/energy efficiency comparisons are reported anywhere in the experiments — only accuracy and firing-rate curves are shown, so the central efficiency claim is essentially unsubstantiated.

Section III-D promises an ablation over decay functions (linear vs. exponential, various γ) for the proposed temporal weighting decoding scheme ("We conducted an ablation study in Sec. IV-C, comparing linear functions and various exponential factors γ"), but Section IV-C (Table III) only ablates initialization and average pooling; the temporal weighting method itself — one of the three headline contributions — is never ablated or compared against alternative decoding schemes (e.g., simple TTFS latency decoding, max-based decoding), leaving its actual contribution unverified.

Results are reported as single numbers with no error bars, standard deviations, or multiple-seed runs, making it impossible to assess whether the reported gains (e.g., 90.1% vs 89.3%, or 91.61% vs 90.35%) are statistically meaningful given typical run-to-run variance in SNN training.

The core initialization derivation closely follows established variance-preserving initialization logic (à la Kaiming/He and prior fluctuation-driven SNN initialization work such as Rossbroich et al., cited as [55]); the novelty is largely in adapting the derivation to the TTFS single-spike assumption, which is a comparatively narrow theoretical extension rather than a fundamentally new idea, and the paper does not clearly differentiate its derivation from directly related prior initialization work for SNNs.

Architectural and implementation details are incomplete for reproducibility: "SCNN1" in Table II is never spelled out with full layer specifications matching the earlier described SCNN architecture, and hyperparameters (e.g., γ selection rationale beyond "we set γ=2", threshold values, exact firing mask/reset details for deeper nets) are not fully specified; no code release is mentioned.

The assumption underlying the initialization derivation — that each neuron fires exactly one spike per forward pass, enforced by setting the threshold to −∞ at the last timestep — is a strong idealization that may not hold for the input/first layer (where inputs are often not binary spikes) nor uniformly across all layers in deeper or convolutional networks, and this discrepancy is not empirically validated beyond the shallow architectures tested.

Presentation quality is weak: Figures 8 and 9 share an identical, uninformative caption ("Comparison of the convergence speed and final performance of the network") despite depicting different quantities (accuracy vs. firing rate), and there are multiple typos ("disminishing," "choice" for "chose," "seem" for "see"), suggesting insufficient proofreading.

The claimed SOTA comparisons omit several relevant recent TTFS/temporal-coding baselines evaluated on more challenging benchmarks, and the comparison table entries reuse different underlying architectures (e.g., 600 vs 400 hidden units) across baselines, which somewhat confounds the fairness of head-to-head accuracy comparisons.

strengths: The paper provides a clear theoretical derivation (Eq. 8-21) that identifies two concrete failure modes in TTFS neuron training under standard Kaiming initialization: exponential signal diminishing with depth and imbalanced/skewed membrane potential distributions. The derivation of the proposed variance-preserving initialization (σ^2 = T/n) follows a similar rigor style to the original Kaiming derivation and is empirically supported by Figures 1, 2, 4, and 5.

The temporal weighting decoding scheme is a simple, well-motivated modification (exponential decay weighting of spike outputs) that is compatible with BPTT and directly targets the known issue that later spikes in TTFS carry less information.

The re-examination of pooling layers is a useful, previously overlooked practical insight for TTFS-coded SNNs: max-pooling can violate the single-spike/temporal-sum constraint, whereas average pooling preserves it and can be algebraically fused with subsequent convolutions, reducing inference overhead.
The ablation study (Table III) cleanly isolates the individual and joint contributions of the initialization scheme and average pooling, showing consistent incremental improvements.
The related work section is thorough and situates the contribution reasonably well against ANN-to-SNN conversion, direct training, and prior neural coding and initialization literature.
weaknesses: There is an unexplained inconsistency between the reported MNIST result in the text (98.2%) and in Table I (99.2%*, with an unexplained asterisk), which undermines confidence in the reported numbers and suggests inadequate proofreading or an unresolved reporting issue.

Empirical validation is restricted to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, both small, low-resolution, near-saturated benchmarks; no results are shown on more challenging datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10/100, neuromorphic datasets) that are standard in the TTFS/SNN literature, which limits the ability to assess whether the proposed initialization and decoding scale to deeper or more complex networks despite claims about 'deeper networks' (the deepest network tested is only 5 layers).

No error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported for any of the main results or ablations, making it hard to judge whether the improvements (e.g., 0.75-1.4 percentage points) are robust rather than noise, especially given the small absolute gaps to prior SOTA baselines like TQTTFS.

The theoretical derivation of the initialization variance relies on the assumption that 'each neuron fires exactly one spike' (Eq. 20), which is only approximately true; the paper's justification for ignoring violations (forcing a spike at the last time step, then discarding it) is asserted rather than empirically or theoretically validated in detail.

The ablation baseline definitions in Table III are unclear: it is not explained what initialization/pooling scheme is used in the row labeled 'ETTFS' without checkmarks, making the isolated contribution of temporal weighting decoding (a headline contribution) impossible to assess from the ablation, since it is not varied at all in Table III.
No code, hyperparameter details for baselines, or public repository is mentioned, raising reproducibility concerns despite the use of an open framework (SpikingJelly).

Comparisons omit some directly relevant TTFS baselines discussed in the related work (e.g., T2FSNN, TDSNN) despite substantial space devoted to critiquing them, weakening the completeness of the empirical comparison.

strengths: Addresses a clearly identified and practically important problem: TTFS SNNs trained with step-by-step propagation suffer from unstable training and low accuracy, and the paper proposes a coherent set of remedies (initialization, normalization, decoding, pooling) grounded in a theoretical variance analysis.

The derivation of ETTFS-init is mathematically explicit (variance propagation through AMOS neurons) and clearly explains why Kaiming initialization causes signal diminishing in TTFS SNNs as T grows; the fix (scaling variance by T) is simple and well-motivated.

Comprehensive ablation studies (Table 3, Table 5, Figures 5-9) isolate the contribution of each proposed component (init, normalization+affine, pooling, decoding), and results are consistent across four datasets, showing genuine synergistic improvements.

The empirical results show consistent and substantial accuracy gains over baselines/prior TTFS methods (TQ-TTFS, S4NN, BS4NN, STiDi-BP, etc.) on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, and DVS Gesture, including the first reported TTFS accuracy on DVS Gesture, along with reduced inference time-steps.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: architecture tables, hyperparameters, and training details are provided in supplementary material, and the SpikingJelly framework is used for implementation.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation of ETTFS-init assumes independence between input spikes S^{l-1} and weights W^l and treats spike statistics as i.i.d./uncorrelated across neurons; this is a common but strong simplifying assumption (as in Kaiming/Xavier) whose validity for TTFS spike trains with strict one-spike temporal correlation is not empirically verified beyond the specific 5-layer toy analysis in Figure 5.

Comparisons to prior work are somewhat uneven: some baselines are reproduced by the authors (TQ-TTFS on CIFAR10/DVS, marked with †) while most are taken directly from other papers with different training budgets/augmentations (extensive data augmentation such as mixup/cutmix/autoaugment used only for the proposed method per Table 6), raising concerns about a fully fair comparison and whether the observed gains are partly attributable to stronger augmentation/training recipes rather than the core algorithmic contributions alone.

The pooling analysis (Section 3.5) is somewhat overstated as a 're-evaluation'; the argument that max-pooling can violate the one-spike constraint is intuitively obvious and the mathematical treatment (Eq. 35-36) is fairly trivial, yet it is presented as a major contribution.

The temporal weighting decoding hyperparameter (decay type and γ) shows inconsistent, dataset-dependent optimal settings (Figure 9, Table 4) with no principled way to select them a priori, and the paper acknowledges this as 'empirical optimization without generalizable guidelines,' which weakens the generality of this component.

Energy-efficiency and latency claims are based on time-step counts and parameter counts only; no direct measurement or simulation of actual energy consumption or physical latency on real or simulated neuromorphic hardware is provided to substantiate claims about neuromorphic hardware suitability.

The overall novelty is somewhat incremental — mostly systematic adaptation/combination of standard deep learning techniques (variance-preserving initialization, weight normalization with affine transform, weighted temporal aggregation) to the TTFS setting, rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic or theoretical insight.

Scalability to larger, more complex datasets (e.g., ImageNet) is not evaluated; the paper explicitly defers this to future work, leaving open whether the proposed framework generalizes beyond the relatively small-scale benchmarks tested.

strengths: The paper provides a clear, self-consistent theoretical derivation (variance propagation analysis) motivating the ETTFS-init scheme, extending Xavier/He-style analysis to the specific constraints of TTFS (one-spike) neuron dynamics; the derivation is given in detail in the appendix.

Comprehensive ablation studies (Table 3/5, Figures 5-9) isolate the contribution of each proposed component (initialization, weight normalization with affine transform, temporal weighting decoding, pooling choice), and each shows a measurable, monotonic accuracy improvement on Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR10/DVS Gesture.

The pooling re-evaluation (average- vs max-pooling) is a simple but useful practical observation directly tied to preserving the one-spike invariant, with a clean mathematical justification in the appendix.

The paper reports state-of-the-art accuracy among directly-trained TTFS SNNs across four datasets and is the first (to the authors' claim) to report TTFS SNN accuracy on DVS Gesture, together with a large reduction in average inference time-steps versus the TQ-TTFS baseline.
Reasonable reproducibility support: architecture tables, hyperparameter tables, and a statement that code/logs/weights are included in supplementary material.
weaknesses: Significance of the contribution is questionable in absolute terms: even with the proposed framework, TTFS SNN accuracy remains clearly below conversion-based methods using larger backbones (e.g., 90.56% vs 92.72% on CIFAR10 with VGG-16) and far below standard directly-trained (non-TTFS) SNNs/ANNs on these benchmarks; the paper does not contextualize whether the sparsity/energy benefits actually justify this accuracy gap with any hardware-level energy measurement, leaving the core motivating claim (energy efficiency) unverified empirically.

The main baseline comparison (TQ-TTFS) is self-reproduced by the authors for CIFAR10 and DVS Gesture, yielding a suspiciously low 67.47% on CIFAR10 versus the paper's 90.56% — a >20-point gap that raises concerns about whether the baseline was properly tuned; without the original TQ-TTFS numbers on these datasets from the original authors, it is hard to assess whether the comparison is fair or whether the baseline was under-optimized.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the initialization method is a direct extension of classic Xavier/He derivations to a slightly different forward model, weight normalization is an established technique repurposed here, and the temporal weighting decoding is a straightforward differentiable weighted sum substituting for argmin — the combination is useful engineering but each individual piece is conceptually modest.

No indication of multiple runs, variance, or confidence intervals is given for any reported accuracy number; all results appear to be single-run point estimates, which is a concern for a paper making fine-grained accuracy comparisons (e.g., 0.1-1% differences in ablations) as its central evidence.

There is a train/inference mismatch (forced spike at last timestep during training vs. free step-by-step inference with early stopping) that is not carefully analyzed for its effect on the reported latency/accuracy trade-off, despite being central to the framework's behavior.

The weight-decay/temporal-decoding hyperparameter (γ, exponential vs linear) shows inconsistent, non-generalizable behavior across datasets (Fig. 9, Table 4), and the paper acknowledges this ('dataset-specific behavior suggests empirical optimization without generalizable guidelines'), undermining the claimed generality of the decoding contribution.

Minor presentation issues: numbering/cross-referencing errors (e.g., Section 4.2.6 refers to 'Table 5' when the relevant component-ablation table is actually Table 3), and dense notation throughout that could be streamlined for readability.

strengths: Provides a principled theoretical derivation (ETTFS-init) that explains and fixes a concrete signal-diminishing pathology of Kaiming initialization in TTFS SNNs, with clean mean/variance derivations included in the supplementary material.

Comprehensive, well-organized ablation study (Table 3, Figures 5-9) that cleanly isolates the contribution of each proposed component (init, normalization+affine, pooling choice, decoding), supporting the causal claims made in the paper.

Strong empirical results: achieves new SOTA among directly-trained TTFS SNNs on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and reports the first TTFS SNN accuracy on DVS Gesture, along with substantially reduced inference time-steps compared to the TQ-TTFS baseline.

The pooling re-evaluation (average- vs max-pooling) is a simple but practically important and previously overlooked insight specific to the one-spike constraint of TTFS coding, with a clear mathematical justification in the appendix.

Good attention to neuromorphic-hardware relevance: step-by-step vs layer-by-layer propagation latency analysis, discussion of fused weights for inference, and compatibility with hardware that only supports average pooling.
Reproducibility is reasonably well supported: detailed hyperparameter tables, exact network architectures, and a statement that code/weights/logs are included in supplementary material.
weaknesses: The initialization derivation is done for fully-connected layers under an idealized one-spike/independence assumption; its extension to convolutional layers (with weight sharing and spatial correlation between inputs) is asserted (Nl = Cin·Nkernel) but not rigorously justified.

The large jump in accuracy from adding the learnable affine transform (Table 3, e.g., +1.29% on Fashion-MNIST) suggests that a nontrivial part of the empirical gain may stem from added representational capacity/learnable scaling rather than purely from the theoretically motivated variance-stabilization argument; this is not discussed critically.

Comparisons across methods in Table 1 use different network architectures reused from prior papers, which aids fairness in some respects but complicates isolating whether gains come from the proposed framework or from architecture/dataset augmentation choices (e.g., heavy CIFAR10 augmentation: mixup, cutmix, autoaugment) not necessarily used by baselines.

The gamma hyperparameter and choice between linear/exponential decay for temporal weighting decoding require per-dataset tuning with no generalizable guideline, as the authors themselves acknowledge, limiting practical plug-and-play usability.

No explicit energy/hardware measurement is provided; efficiency claims rest solely on inferred time-step counts and spike counts rather than actual measured or simulated energy consumption on neuromorphic hardware.

The forced single spike at the last time-step during training (Eq. 4) versus free-running step-by-step inference introduces a train/inference mismatch whose impact on accuracy/latency trade-offs is not analyzed in depth.
Minor presentation issues, e.g., inconsistent table referencing in Section 4.2.6 (text cites 'Table 5' while apparently referring to the content of Table 3).
